items.stem: On a dataset where 95 percent of samples are class A, a model predicts class A every time. Why is 95 percent accuracy misleading?

options.text: It ignores performance on the rare class, which may be the one of interest
options.rationale: Correct: accuracy hides complete failure on the minority class.

options.text: Accuracy cannot be computed for biological data
options.rationale: Accuracy is computable; it is just a poor summary here.

options.text: 95 percent is actually a poor accuracy
options.rationale: The problem is the choice of metric, not the number.

options.text: The model must be overfitting the minority class
options.rationale: It never predicts the minority class at all.

items.explanation: Correct: accuracy hides complete failure on the minority class.

items.stem: Which TWO practices help prevent data leakage in a biological machine-learning study? (Select TWO.)

options.text: Fitting preprocessing such as scaling only on the training fold
options.rationale: Correct: fitting on the training fold avoids peeking at test data.

options.text: Grouping related samples so they stay within one fold
options.rationale: Correct: grouped splits stop correlated samples leaking across folds.

options.text: Choosing hyperparameters using the test set
options.rationale: That leaks test information into the model.

options.text: Reporting the best of many test runs

items.explanation: Correct: fitting on the training fold avoids peeking at test data.

items.stem: Samples come from distinct donors. Which validation choice best estimates real-world performance?

options.text: Grouped cross-validation that keeps each donor within one fold
options.rationale: Correct: donor-grouped folds stop the model memorising a donor.

options.text: A random split that ignores donor identity
options.rationale: That leaks donor-specific signal across folds.
Validation is required for an honest estimate.

items.explanation: Correct: donor-grouped folds stop the model memorising a donor.
